questions.question: What does the power set $\mathcal P(A)$ contain?
options: All elements that are not in $A$.
questions.explanation: By definition, $\mathcal P(A)=\{B:B\subseteq A\}$, the set of every subset of $A$.
questions.source_support: Definition: $2^A=\{B:B\subseteq A\}$.

An object outside $A$ cannot appear in any subset of $A$.

questions.question: Which two subsets are always included in $\mathcal P(A)$?
questions.explanation: The empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself. Therefore $\varnothing,A\in\mathcal P(A)$.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: the power set includes the empty choice and the full set itself.

questions.question: If a finite set has $n$ elements, how many elements does its power set have?
questions.explanation: Each of the $n$ elements has two independent choices—include or exclude—so the total number of subsets is $2^n$.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: if $A$ has $n$ elements, then $2^A$ has $2^n$ elements.

Because $\varnothing$ is always an element of $A$.

questions.question: What is the power set $\mathcal P(\varnothing)$?

questions.explanation: The empty set has exactly one subset, itself. Thus $\mathcal P(\varnothing)=\{\varnothing\}$, a singleton.

questions.question: If $A=\{a,b\}$, which is $\mathcal P(A)$?
questions.explanation: The four subsets are obtained by choosing neither element, only $a$, only $b$, or both: $\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\}$.
questions.source_support: Example: if $A=\{a,b\}$, then $2^A=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\}\}$.

questions.question: What is $\mathcal P(\{\varnothing\})$?
questions.explanation: The one-element set $\{\varnothing\}$ has two subsets: choose none to get $\varnothing$, or choose its sole element to get $\{\varnothing\}$.

questions.question: Why is the notation $2^A$ natural for a power set?
options: It means $A$ must be a set of numbers.
It means the power set contains exactly two subsets for every set.
For each element of $A$, a subset makes one of two choices: include it or exclude it.
It means every element of $A$ is multiplied by $2$.

questions.source_support: Relevant result: if $A$ has $n$ elements, then $2^A$ has $2^n$ elements.

questions.question: What does Cantor's theorem say about the size of $\mathcal P(A)$?
options: It always has the same cardinality as $A$.
It is smaller than $A$ whenever $A$ is infinite.
It has larger cardinality only when $A$ is finite.
It has strictly larger cardinality than $A$.

questions.source_support: Relevant result: for any set $A$, $2^A$ has strictly larger cardinality than $A$.

questions.question: Cantor's theorem gives $|A|<|\mathcal P(A)|$ for every set $A$. Which conclusion does this rule out?

There is no subset of $\mathcal P(A)$.
There is no function from $A$ to $\mathcal P(A)$.
